originalTitle: News live: limits on smartglasses being considered, Plibersek says; missing Australian woman located safely in Nepal
content: Joyce explains One Nation’s migration policy with sheep and cattle Barnaby Joyce has used sheep and cattle to illustrate his claim that One Nation wants to cut net overseas migration to 130,000 people without counting short-stay visas. Pauline Hanson earlier this week said a One Nation government would aim for net migration of 130,000, plus workers on Pacific Australia labour mobility stream (Palm) visas. Asked by the News24 (formerly Sky) host, Andrew Clennell, if Hanson’s position was nonsensical, Joyce said: No it’s not. … Short-term visa stay and things such as the Palm scheme, and Pauline’s quite right, are not counted in the net overseas migration number, overwhelmingly – small portion are – because they don’t stay for 12 months. They stay generally for a period of nine. So it’s like saying to someone, how many sheep have you got. You go, ‘well, I’ve got, you know, 5000.’ Oh, yes, and how many cattle have you got? ‘Oh, well, I’ve got 2000.’ Oh, so you’ve got 7000 all up. So, no, no. Two different things. Sheep, one, cattle, the other. Net overseas migration, one; Palm scheme, short term visas, another. People have not asked us the net overseas visa number and I wouldn’t really know, to be quite frank, what that would be. Net overseas migration was about 301,000 in 2025. The Australian Bureau of Statistics calculates that figure by assuming people have arrived in (or departed from) Australia if they spent at least 12 of 16 months in (or out of) the country. The Palm scheme gives people from Pacific countries working rights in agricultural industries in rural and regional Australia. Some travellers can stay in Australia for up to four years under the scheme. A 13-year-old boy from Childers in Queensland has died in hospital from injuries he suffered in an e-scooter crash last week. A statement from the Queensland police said the boy sustained serious head injuries in the single-vehicle crash about 6pm on Wednesday. He was airlifted from the town, near Bundaberg in central Queensland, to the Queensland Children’s hospital in a critical condition. He died in hospital on Saturday. Police said their investigations into the crash were ongoing. Plibersek says One Nation byelection win ‘on state issues’ Tanya Plibersek has downplayed One Nation’s victory in the Secret Harbour state byelection in Western Australia as a local vote fought on state issues. Plibersek said Labor would look at “any outcome like this” and learn from it, acknowledging a lot of Australians were under pressure. She said Labor’s housing policies, Medicare investment, support for wage growth and tax cuts would “make a difference”. Pauline Hanson, One Nation’s federal leader, has been the face of the party across state campaigns and has targeted Anthony Albanese. Asked if the prime minister was hurting the Labor party’s electoral prospects, Plibersek said: Oh, this is a state election run on state issues, and I think they’re the predominant issues. However, it is important that all of us have a good look at the results here, and think about what more we need to do to communicate the fact that the Labor party is the only party, focused on real delivery to take pressure off ordinary Australians. Read more about the byelection here: Cabinet never discussed refugee cuts, says Plibersek Tanya Plibersek has said cabinet never discussed cutting Australia’s refugee intake after debate and confusion within Labor came into public view this week. The Financial Review on Thursday reported the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was planning to cut intake of 20,000 arrivals to 13,750 in 2027-28. The prime minister declared the figure would stay at 20,000 after Labor MPs and refugee advocates reacted angrily. Asked on the ABC’s Insiders if the government had considered a cut to the refugee intake, Plibersek said: No, I don’t really know where this story came from. We reconfirmed our number as recently as a month ago at the national conference. There was certainly no discussion in cabinet. She said the 20,000-a-year figure was a “permanent commitment”. The party’s most recent national conference voted to approve a statement that read: Labor will seek, in the short term, to maintain Australia’s government funded humanitarian intake numbers at 20,000 places per year while also continuing to aspire to achieving 27,000 places per year. Tanya Plibersek says the government is reviewing the import of smartglasses, dubbed by some as “pervert glasses”. She said she “absolutely” had a problem with the devices, speaking on Insiders. I think it is really concerning when tech companies just, come up with these products and release them without thought of how they can be misused. … I don’t think it’s right to be able to walk up to someone and film an interaction without them knowing that the interactions being filmed. Plibersek said the government was “considering very closely” limits on importing the glasses but did not specify what action was planned. She said: The attorney general has asked the privacy commissioner to look specifically at these glasses, and the attorney general will have more to say about the import of the glasses soon. Schools scared parents will object to sex education, says Plibersek Tanya Plibersek has said some schools are scared to give young people “frank” education about sex and respectful relationships. Speaking on Insiders, the social services minister said: I think there’s a lot of schools out there who don’t want to have frank conversations with young people, because they’re worried that parents will object to their children and young people being spoken to directly. I think we are well beyond that. We know that children, as young as 10, are seeing pornography before they’ve had their first kiss. They’re getting their sex education from pornography.
